To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the Sun's magnetic helicity is conserved locally but not globally, that magnetic helicity does not play a significant role in determining where reconnection occurs, and that the Sun's coronal magnetic field does not relax completely down to its minimum energy state.
(1) the Sun's magnetic helicity budget is in conflict with Taylor's relaxation theory, and (2) the magnetic field in the solar atmosphere is not relaxing towards the minimum energy state.

the solar corona is not in a state of minimum energy, the magnetic energy of the solar corona cannot be used to drive solar eruptions, and the Sun's magnetic helicity is not conserved in the solar corona.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of magnetic helicity in determining the nature of magnetic reconnection and its consequences for solar activity.
the fundamental question of why the solar atmosphere is so hot.
the role of helicity in determining the structure of the coronal magnetic field.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
helicity plays only an insignificant role in the dynamics of the Sun's magnetic fields.
conservation of global magnetic helicity does not play a dominant role in determining the structure of the solar corona, the nature of solar flares, or the evolution of the Sun's magnetic fields.
the role of helicity conservation in magnetic reconnection is negligible.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the magnetic energy in the corona is not conserved.
helicity is important in the Sun's atmosphere, but that it is only a small part of the overall story.
the Sun's magnetic energy is stored in a very small number of flux ropes, which are anchored to the Sun by their footpoints.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the Sun's magnetic energy and helicity are not conserved in the long run and that the solar dynamo must continually generate new magnetic flux and helicity to sustain the solar cycle.
the Sun's coronal magnetic field does not relax to the minimum energy, global-helicity-conserving state predicted by Taylor's theory, and the consequences of this are far reaching.
the magnetic energy density of the solar atmosphere is so high that it is not possible to reconfigure the field in such a way that all the energy can be dissipated by resistive processes.
